correctness.rationale: For the simple unit cycle, the permitted additions are all nonedges. There are 5,9,14,20,27 at n=5,6,7,8,9, so the stated 5281 configurations of size zero through three is exact. The Laplacian cofactor counts trees by Kirchhoff, and the second formula follows from the rank-update determinant lemma and polarization of cycle resistance R_uv=|u-v|(n-|u-v|)/n. I independently enumerated every (n−1)-edge subset of each augmented graph, counting it exactly when cycle-free, which at this cardinality is equivalent to being a tree. I propagated all local maxima separately for each reachable prefix, and separately enumerated all globally maximizing triples. The global maxima at n=5,…,9 were 45,81,117,168,240; every greedy triple for the first four orders attained the corresponding maximum. For n=9, all 18 distinct greedies had 235 trees, the three listed labeled triples were precisely the global optima, and there was no overlap. The gap is 5/240=1/48. The only smaller simple cycles, C3 and C4, do not admit the budget. The verifier's docstring briefly uses an obsolete filename; the source file and the Verification instructions correctly name verify.py.
residual_risks: Does not assert greedy behavior for n≥10, other budgets, weighted chords or nonsimple cycles.

originality.rationale: Credit existing coverage of the greedy algorithm and the global maxima at n=6–9, including the 240-tree nine-cycle optimum. Pass the distinct claim that nine is the first order with tie-robust three-chord greedy failure, with the complete 18-triple greedy census and exact gap, not the global value alone. No inspected prior result implies this finite boundary and equality profile. The frozen bibliography's location for the three-chord comparison should be §3, Table 3, not §§2.2–2.3. Also, it is log tree count, not raw tree count, that is submodular; maximizing either gives the same greedy choices. These literature corrections do not change the mathematical finding.

value.rationale: A natural base graph and small fixed budget give a first exact test of whether an established greedy design algorithm can always be rescued by choosing favorable ties. Exhaustively ruling that out at the first possible order, while confirming every tie branch earlier, supplies a useful counterexample and a sharp finite benchmark. The mathematical distinction is the failure of exactness for all ties, not the small relative loss or a claim of practical design improvement.
residual_risks: No universal approximation improvement or structural statement for longer cycles follows from the finite cutoff.
